::: {.chapter-goal}
#### In this chapter
You will add pattern to spectrum. Grey level co-occurrence matrix features let a classifier separate a planted monoculture from a structurally complex natural stand when the two reflect almost identically, which is the confusion no amount of spectral engineering can fix.
:::

## Two forests, one signature

An oil palm plantation and a natural mangrove stand can have identical mean reflectance in every band. Both are dense broadleaf canopy, both photosynthesise vigorously, both hold similar leaf water. Chapter [-@sec-indices]'s indices, which are all functions of per pixel reflectance, cannot separate them because there is nothing in the per pixel reflectance to separate.

What differs is **arrangement**. Palm is planted on a regular grid with uniform crown size and uniform spacing. Natural mangrove has crowns of many sizes, irregular gaps, tidal creeks cutting through it and no repeating geometry at all.

A human interpreter sees that difference instantly, and does so without measuring a single pixel value. Texture analysis is the attempt to give a classifier the same information.

## What GLCM measures

The grey level co-occurrence matrix, introduced by Haralick in 1973 and still the standard, works on pairs rather than on individual pixels.

For a given neighbourhood, it counts how often a pixel of value $i$ sits adjacent to a pixel of value $j$, building a matrix of those co-occurrence counts. Statistics computed from that matrix describe the local arrangement.

The intuition is worth holding onto. A smooth uniform canopy produces co-occurrences clustered near the matrix diagonal, because neighbouring pixels have similar values. A broken heterogeneous canopy spreads them out, because a bright sunlit crown frequently sits next to a dark shadowed gap.

## The four measures worth keeping

`glcmTexture()` returns eighteen bands per input band. They are heavily redundant; several are near duplicates. Four carry most of the independent information.

| Measure | Question it answers | High values mean |
|---|---|---|
| **Contrast** | How different are neighbouring pixels? | Broken canopy with gaps, high local variation |
| **Entropy** | How disordered is the arrangement? | Natural regeneration, no repeating pattern |
| **ASM** | How uniform is it? (inverse of entropy) | Smooth, homogeneous canopy |
| **Correlation** | How predictable is a pixel from its neighbour? | Periodic structure, such as planting rows |

**Entropy** is usually the single most discriminating band for the plantation versus natural question, because order is precisely what planting imposes and precisely what natural regeneration lacks.

**Correlation** is the one people overlook and it is the most direct test for a plantation, because a planted grid is genuinely periodic in a way nothing natural is.

## The preparation nobody documents

`glcmTexture()` has two hard requirements and neither produces a useful error when violated.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common failure: passing float input
GLCM requires **integer** input. Pass a float band and you get nonsense rather than an exception. Since Chapter [-@sec-cloud] rescaled reflectance to floats between 0 and 1, the band must be rescaled and cast before use.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common failure: the wrong number of grey levels
GLCM builds an $N \times N$ matrix where $N$ is the number of distinct values.

Cast 0 to 1 float reflectance straight to integer and you get **two** levels. The matrix is 2 by 2 and carries no information.

Multiply by 10000 first and you get thousands of levels, a matrix with millions of cells, and a computation that exhausts memory.

Quantise to 0 to 255. That is enough levels to capture structure, small enough to compute, and it is what the original formulation assumed.
:::

Run it on **one band**, not the whole stack. Eighteen output bands per input means ten inputs give 180 texture bands, which will exhaust memory and add mostly redundant information, since texture in adjacent spectral bands is highly correlated.

Near infrared is the usual choice for vegetation, because it has the greatest contrast between sunlit crown and shadowed gap, so canopy structure is most visible there. For urban work a visible band often works better, because shadow between buildings carries the structure.

![Two synthetic canopies with deliberately matched mean reflectance. Only the arrangement differs, and GLCM entropy separates them: 4.95 for the planted grid against 8.25 for the natural stand.](images/glcm-texture.png){#fig-texture}

The means in @fig-texture are matched on purpose. Every spectral index computed on those two images returns the same answer. Entropy nearly doubles.

## Window size is an ecological decision

The `size` parameter is a radius in pixels, so the analysis window is $(2 \times size + 1)$ square. At Sentinel-2's 10 metres:

| `size` | Window | Ground | Suits |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3 × 3 | 30 m | Smaller than one large crown. Measures noise more than structure. |
| 3 | 7 × 7 | 70 m | Spans several crowns. Good default for canopy type. |
| 7 | 15 × 15 | 150 m | Spans a stand. Good for land cover type, blurs boundaries between them. |

The rule: the window must be **large enough to contain several instances of the pattern** you want to detect, and **small enough not to straddle a boundary** between two cover types.

Match it to crown diameter rather than to a default. Mangrove crowns run roughly 5 to 15 metres, so a 70 metre window spans five to fourteen crowns, which is enough to characterise their arrangement without averaging across a boundary.

## Test before you trust

Do not add texture bands on faith. They are expensive, and in some landscapes they contribute nothing.

The test takes two minutes. Sample the texture bands at your training points from Chapter [-@sec-sampling], then plot two of them against each other coloured by class. If the two classes that confuse each other separate along entropy, the bands have earned their place. If they overlap completely, you have added four bands of computation and no information, and you should drop them.

This is the same discipline as the histogram test in Chapter [-@sec-indices], applied to a different feature family. The general principle: every predictor should be able to justify itself before it enters the stack, and after it enters, Chapter [-@sec-supervised]'s feature importance chart should confirm it is still contributing.

::: {.callout-tip}
## From the field
Zoom to a boundary between plantation and natural forest. In true colour it may be nearly invisible. In entropy it should be obvious.

If it is not, one of two things is true. Either your window size is wrong for the crown size, which you fix. Or the two stands are genuinely more similar than you assumed, which is itself a finding worth knowing before you build a classifier on the assumption that they differ.
:::

## The relationship to object based analysis

Chapter [-@sec-obia] reaches a similar place by a different route.

Texture measures variation within a moving window of fixed size and shape. Object based analysis segments the image into coherent regions first, then measures variation within each region, which adapts to the actual shape of things on the ground.

The object based version is more principled: a standard deviation computed within a real stand means more than one computed within an arbitrary 70 metre square that may straddle two stands.

Texture is cheaper, simpler, and works as an ordinary band in an ordinary pixel based workflow. Start here. Move to Chapter [-@sec-obia] when the fixed window becomes the limitation, which you will recognise when texture works in the interior of stands and fails at their edges.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Run at `size` 1, 3 and 7 over the same plantation boundary. Find the size at which the boundary is clearest and relate it to crown diameter.
2. Skip the integer cast and run on the float band. Describe how the failure presents itself.
3. Quantise to 32 levels instead of 255. What is gained and what is lost?
4. Run GLCM on NDVI rather than B8. Does the structural signal improve, and can you say why?
5. Sample your texture bands at training points and plot entropy against contrast, coloured by class. Decide, on that evidence, whether to keep them.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

**1.** At `size` 1 (30 m window) the texture is mostly speckle of single crowns and the boundary is noisy. At `size` 3 (70 m) the planted grid and the natural stand separate cleanly, because the window spans roughly five to fourteen crowns of 5-15 m. At `size` 7 (150 m) the contrast is strong but the boundary is smeared across about 75 m on each side. The clearest boundary is usually at the window that spans several crowns but less than the stand width: here `size` 3.

**2.** No exception is raised. With 0-1 float reflectance cast implicitly, nearly every pixel falls into one or two grey levels, so the co-occurrence matrix is degenerate: entropy and contrast come out constant or near zero across the scene, and the texture layer looks blank or banded. The failure presents as a uniform, useless layer rather than an error, which is why it survives.

**3.** 32 levels make the matrix 32 × 32 instead of 256 × 256, so the computation is far faster and less memory-hungry, and the statistics are more stable in small windows (fewer empty cells). What is lost is subtle variation: two canopies whose brightness differs by less than one 32-level step look identical. For separating planted from natural stands 32 is often enough; for fine condition differences keep 255.

**4.** Usually yes, modestly. NDVI is a ratio, so it removes the illumination and shading variation between sunlit and shaded crowns that B8 carries; the texture then reflects arrangement of vegetation vs gaps rather than sun-shadow pattern. But NDVI saturates in dense canopy, so within a closed natural stand it varies little and texture can weaken. Keep the index on which the two classes' entropy histograms separate better.

**5.** If the classes form separate clouds in the entropy-contrast plot, for example plantation at low entropy and natural stand at high, the texture bands carry information the spectral bands do not, and you keep them. If the clouds overlap completely, they add only correlated noise and computation: drop them. Decide with the plot, then confirm with feature importance in Chapter [-@sec-supervised].
:::
